privacy.title: Privacy
intro: JuggerHub is a community site for Jugger players. To make it work we hold some information about you — your email address, your profile, your messages, and which teams and events you're part of.

This page says what we hold, why we hold it, who else sees it, and what you can do about it. We've tried to write it in plain language rather than the usual wall of clauses. Where something is awkward, we've said so rather than smoothing it over.

controller.heading: Who is responsible
body: JuggerHub is run by Jan Niklas Rösch, Lattenkamp 12, 22299 Hamburg, Germany — the controller for everything described on this page.
If you have a question about your data, or want to exercise any of the rights further down, write to hello@juggerhub.com. A person reads it — there is no ticketing system.

account.heading: Your account
body: When you register we store your email address, a username, and your password. The password is never stored as you typed it — only as an argon2 hash, which cannot be turned back into your password.
We also store your account's state (active, suspended, or banned) and when it last changed, so moderation decisions are auditable.

Each time you sign in we record a session, and that record includes the IP address the sign-in came from. We keep it as a security measure: it's what lets us tell a legitimate session from a stolen one. It is not used for analytics or for anything else.
We need this to give you an account at all, so the basis is the contract between you and us.

email.heading: Email we send you
body: We send email for things the site can't work without — confirming your address, resetting your password, invitations, and notifications you've asked for. You control which notification emails you get in your notification settings.
Email is delivered by a provider on our behalf; see "Who else processes your data" below. That provider necessarily sees your address and the content of the message.
The basis is the contract for account email, and your consent for anything optional.

profile.heading: Your profile
body: Your profile holds what you choose to put in it: display name, the pompfen you play, a short description, your home city, and a photo if you upload one.

Your profile is private by default. Signed-in members can find you; nobody who isn't signed in can. If you switch your profile to public, it becomes readable by anyone who has the direct link to it — that is what public means here. It does not get listed anywhere for search engines, but it also isn't secret once the link exists.
You can change or empty any of these fields at any time, and switching back to private takes effect immediately.

location.heading: Where you're based
body: You can set a home city so other players can find teams and events near you. We store the city you pick, not a precise location — there is no GPS, no address, and no tracking of where you actually are.
Cities come from a list we ship with the site. Choosing one does not send anything to an outside mapping or geocoding service.

chat.heading: Messages
body: Direct messages, group chats, team chats and admin inquiries are stored on our servers so they're there when you come back. They are not end-to-end encrypted: in principle, someone with database access could read them. We keep that access tightly limited, but we would rather tell you than let you assume otherwise.

One thing that surprises people: when a team is deleted or an event is cancelled, its conversations are not deleted. They're archived as a snapshot, so the people who were in them keep their own history. If you'd rather that didn't happen to a conversation you're in, write to us.
You can block another member, which stops them messaging you.

participation.heading: Teams, events, training and the marketplace
body: We store which teams you're in, which events and training sessions you've signed up for, which parties you've joined, and any mercenary listings or requests you've made.

This is visible to other members — that's the point of it. Your teammates can see you're on the roster; people at an event can see you're going. Treat anything you put here as visible to the community, not as private.
We also store badges and achievements awarded to you, and the notifications generated for you.

eventContacts.heading: Contact details on events
body: An event's organisers can list contact people for it — a name, a role, and optionally a phone number or email address, so attendees know who to reach on the day.

This is the one place where the platform can hold details about someone who does not have a JuggerHub account, because an organiser can type in anybody. If you have been listed as a contact and would rather not be, ask the event's organisers to remove you, or write to us and we will.

These details are visible to members who can see the event. The basis is the organiser's legitimate interest in running the event, and where the contact is a third party, we act on removal requests without argument.

media.heading: Photos you upload
body: If you upload a profile photo, we process it (resize and re-encode it) and store the resulting image file with our cloud storage provider. The original file is not kept.
Images are never served directly from that storage. Every request goes through JuggerHub, which checks whether you're allowed to see the image first. There is no public link to the underlying file.

language.heading: Your language
body: If you're signed in and pick a language, we store that choice on your account so it follows you between devices. If you're not signed in, the choice is stored in your own browser and never reaches us.

analytics.heading: How we measure visits
body: We measure how the site is used, so we know which parts are worth working on. It runs on our own servers — no data goes to Google Analytics or any other outside analytics company.

It sets no cookie and stores nothing on your device. It does not record your account, your username, your email address, or your full IP address. Nothing in the analytics data says who was doing the browsing.

There is one thing we want to be straightforward about, because it's the part people would reasonably object to. We record the address of each page viewed exactly as it is — and some page addresses contain a member's username or a team's name, like /u/alex or /t/wolves. So the analytics data does show which member profiles and team pages were looked at, and when. It never shows who was looking.
We record the path only, never the part of the address after a question mark. That's deliberate: it's where deep links and return addresses live, and those would have carried more than we intended.
If you'd rather not be measured at all, see "How to object" at the end of this page — it takes one browser setting and we honour it.

legalBasis.heading: What we rely on to do this
body: Two questions get muddled together a lot, so we'll take them one at a time.

First: cookie consent. The rule that makes sites ask permission is about storing things on your device. Our analytics stores nothing on your device — no cookie, no local storage, nothing — so that rule simply isn't engaged. The only cookie we set is the one that keeps you signed in, which is necessary for a service you asked for and is exempt. That's why you don't see a cookie banner here. It isn't an oversight, and it isn't us being clever with the wording.

Second: the legal basis for the measuring itself. Because page addresses can name a member or a team, that data is personal data, and it needs a basis regardless of the cookie question. We rely on legitimate interest.

Here is the balancing, so you can judge it rather than take our word for it. Our interest is knowing which parts of a volunteer-run community site are actually used, so limited effort goes where it helps. The impact on you is narrow: nothing identifies you as the viewer, nothing is stored on your device, nothing leaves our servers, the data isn't combined with your account or used to build any profile of you, and it's never used to make a decision about you. What remains is that a page naming you may show up in a list of viewed pages. We think that's proportionate to running the site well — and because it's legitimate interest and not consent, you have an absolute right to object, which we've made a single setting rather than a form.

Everything else on this page rests on the contract between you and us (having an account, being in a team, receiving messages), on your consent where you opted in (optional notification email), or on our legal obligations.

storage.heading: Cookies and what's kept in your browser
body: A sign-in cookie, which is how the site knows you're you. It's set with httpOnly, so JavaScript can't read it. Without it you can't stay signed in.
If you're not signed in and pick a language, that choice is stored in your browser. It stays there and is never sent to us.
That's all. Analytics adds nothing, and there are no advertising, tracking, or third-party cookies of any kind.

processors.heading: Who else processes your data
body: Microsoft Azure hosts the whole application — the servers, the database, and the storage holding uploaded images. Everything we hold is therefore stored on their infrastructure, in their West Europe region (the Netherlands), inside the EU.
Resend delivers our email. They see the recipient address and the message content of anything we send you. This applies to the live site; a local development copy sends nothing anywhere.

That's the complete list, and the absences are worth stating too. There is no third-party analytics service. There is no advertising network. There is no outside mapping or geocoding service — the city list ships with the site. And the fonts are bundled with the site rather than fetched from Google Fonts, so loading a page makes no request to Google.
Where a provider processes data outside the EU, that transfer is covered by the standard contractual clauses in our agreement with them.

retention.heading: How long we keep things
body: We'll be straight with you, because a made-up number would be worse than the truth: JuggerHub has no automatic deletion running today. Nothing expires on a schedule. Your data stays until your account is deleted, and account deletion happens when you ask us for it.
We'd rather say that plainly than publish a retention period the site doesn't actually apply. Building proper retention is on the list.
Analytics data is the one thing that is genuinely limited by design — it holds no identifier for you in the first place, so there is nothing in it to delete on your behalf.

rights.heading: Your rights
body: Under EU data protection law you can ask for a copy of what we hold about you, ask us to correct it, ask us to delete it, ask us to restrict what we do with it, ask for it in a portable form, and object to processing based on legitimate interest.

Right now there is no self-service button for any of this — no export, no delete-my-account control in the settings. We're telling you that rather than pointing you at a feature that doesn't exist. The route is to write to the contact address in the imprint, and we'll do it by hand. Making these self-service is planned work.
The exception is objecting to analytics, which you can do yourself in seconds — see the next section.

You can also complain to a data protection supervisory authority. Ours is the Hamburg Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (Der Hamburgische Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit), Ludwig-Erhard-Str. 22, 20459 Hamburg. You can also go to the authority where you live.

objection.heading: How to object to being measured
body: Turn on "Do Not Track" (or Global Privacy Control) in your browser. That's it — from then on we record nothing at all for you.

You'll usually find it under Settings → Privacy. In Firefox it's "Tell websites not to sell or share my data". In Safari and Brave a similar setting is on by default. In Chrome it's under Privacy and security.
Plenty of sites ignore that signal. We don't: when it's on, no measurement is sent and nothing is recorded. It applies immediately, needs no account, and there's nothing to switch back on.
To object to anything else on this page, write to the contact address in the imprint.
